The initiation (dīkṣā )was a necessary, elaborate and symbolic rite. In the Vedic context also, we find the element of dīkṣā, but it is only as a preliminary ritual qualifying an individual to perform a sacrifice. It has none of the deeper significances that we find in the tantras-tradition where the guru or ācārya (teacher, master) who bestows initiation, plays an all-important role in the spiritual evolution of the aspirant.¹⁵ Hence devotion to God in this approach is supplemented by devotion to the guru; the notion of devotion involves both devata-bhakti and guru-bhakti. And because it is the guru who leads the devotee to Godhead, devotion to him becomes in fact more urgent and important than devotion of Godhead.
Although the Āgama and nigama traditions started out with-such divergent approaches, there was, in course of time, an attempt at appproachment. The tantra borrowed many details from the Vedic tradition and adapted many others. The celebrated Gāyatrī (Ṛgveda,), which was a hymn directed towards the Solar divinity was adapted to suit the needs of the mother-goddess cult. We have, the formula Tripurayaividmahe, bhairavyai dhīmahi, tan no devi pracodayat', after the Vedic Gāyatrī. The hymn of benediction from Ṛgveda (1,89,6) was adapte to the worship of Śakti. Like the Vedic sandhyā ritual, there was instituted a tāntrika-sandhayā involving similar sequences and hymns. Vedic authorities were cited in support of the Kaula rites which appeared rather outlandish.

summary: This section contrasts the role of the guru and initiation (dīkṣā) in Tantric and Vedic traditions. In Tantra, the guru's role is central, involving a deeply significant initiation for the aspirant's spiritual evolution, which elevates devotion to the guru (guru-bhakti) to a position of greater importance than devotion to God. The text also details the process of syncretism, where the Āgama-nigama (Tantric) traditions, despite different origins, borrowed and adapted elements from the Vedic tradition. Examples include the adaptation of the Vedic Gāyatrī mantra for the mother-goddess cult, the use of a Ṛgvedic hymn for Śakti worship, and the creation of a tāntrika-sandhyā ritual modeled on the Vedic one.
key_themes: Guru's role in Tantra vs. Vedic tradition
Syncretism between Tantric (Āgama) and Vedic traditions
Primacy of guru-bhakti (devotion to the guru) in Tantra
Adaptation of Vedic hymns and rituals for Śakti worship
main_arguments: In Tantra, the guru and the initiation (dīkṣā) they bestow are central to an aspirant's spiritual evolution, a role far more significant than the preliminary, sacrificial function of dīkṣā in the Vedic context.
Devotion to the guru (guru-bhakti) in the Tantric tradition becomes more critical than devotion to God (devata-bhakti) because the guru is the direct guide to the divine.

The Tantric traditions engaged in a process of borrowing and reinterpreting elements from the Vedic tradition to serve their own theological and ritual needs, particularly in the context of mother-goddess worship.
methodology: The methodology is primarily comparative and historical. The author compares key concepts like 'dīkṣā' and 'bhakti' across two distinct but related religious systems (Vedic and Tantric). The analysis is historical in that it describes a process of borrowing and adaptation over time, using specific textual examples (such as the Gāyatrī mantra from the Ṛgveda) to demonstrate the syncretic relationship between the two traditions.
historiographical_context: This text engages with the scholarly discussion on the relationship between Vedism and Tantrism in the history of Indian religions. It moves beyond a simple oppositional view, highlighting a complex interaction characterized by syncretism and appropriation. By focusing on how Tantra adapted Vedic forms, the author contributes to the understanding of Tantra's development and its strategies for gaining authority and integrating into the broader religious landscape.
research_questions: How does the significance of initiation (dīkṣā) and the role of the guru differ between the Vedic and Tantric traditions?
What is the relationship between devotion to the guru (guru-bhakti) and devotion to God (devata-bhakti) within the Tantric framework?
In what specific ways did the Tantric tradition borrow from and adapt Vedic rituals and hymns?
